The file uses placeholders. Replace them, here with sed (on macOS use sed -i ''):

cp deploy/kubernetes/ea-hub.yaml ~/ea-hub.yaml
sed -i 's#http://ea-hub.local#https://hub.example.com#g; s#ea-hub.local#hub.example.com#g' ~/ea-hub.yaml
sed -i 's#admin@example.com#admin@yourcompany.com#g' ~/ea-hub.yaml
# only if you use your own registry (Step 3, option 2):
sed -i 's#ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost:latest#registry.example.com/ea-hub-selfhost:1.0.0#g' ~/ea-hub.yaml

If you need the ghcr-pull secret from Step 3, attach it to the namespace's default service account so every pod uses it:

kubectl -n ea-hub patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-pull"}]}'

The Ingress in this file has no ingressClassName, so it uses your cluster's default ingress class. For HTTPS, add a tls: section and the cert-manager annotation by hand, or use Path A.

docs.title: 7B. Apply and wait
docs.text:
The resources in this file carry no namespace, so always pass -n ea-hub:

kubectl apply -n ea-hub -f ~/ea-hub.yaml
kubectl -n ea-hub rollout status deploy/ea-hub --timeout=10m
kubectl -n ea-hub get pods

The expected output is the same as in 7A.

docs.title: Step 8 — Open the site and sign in
docs.text:
With a domain: open https://hub.example.com.

Without a domain / ingress, forward a local port:

kubectl -n ea-hub port-forward svc/ea-hub 8080:80
# then open http://localhost:8080

When testing like this, set appUrl: http://localhost:8080 (Path A) or APP_URL (Path B) so links and uploaded images use the right address.

Health check: the app answers on /healthz:

curl https://hub.example.com/healthz
{"ok":true,"database":"ok"}

Sign in: go to /admin and use the admin e-mail and password from Step 5:

After signing in you land on the dashboard:

First things to do:

  1. My account → change password. Then remove admin.password from my-values.yaml (Path A) or admin-password from your Secret file. The account already exists, so the old value is no longer needed.
  2. Settings → General: site name, logo and contact details.
  3. Settings → Notifications (needs SMTP) and Settings → AI assistant if you use them.
  4. Back up the Secret. Without app-encryption-key, saved keys and sessions cannot be read after a restore: 
    kubectl -n ea-hub get secret ea-hub -o yaml > ea-hub-secret-backup.yaml   # store it somewhere safe

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Path A:

git pull
helm upgrade ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml --set image.tag=<new-version>

Path B: take the new deploy/kubernetes/ea-hub.yaml, repeat 6B, then kubectl apply -n ea-hub -f ~/ea-hub.yaml.

Database changes are applied automatically by the init container before the new version starts. Your data and files are kept.

docs.title: Rotate secrets
docs.text:
The generated passwords live in the release Secret (ea-hub) and are kept on upgrades, so you rotate them by changing the Secret and restarting. Never rotate app-encryption-key: sessions, signed links and saved keys depend on it.

new() { openssl rand -hex 24; }
# app database password: the migrate init container sets it in PostgreSQL on start
kubectl -n ea-hub patch secret ea-hub -p "{\"stringData\":{\"app-db-password\":\"$(new)\"}}"
# scheduled-jobs secret and /metrics token
kubectl -n ea-hub patch secret ea-hub -p "{\"stringData\":{\"cron-secret\":\"$(new)\",\"metrics-token\":\"$(new)\"}}"
kubectl -n ea-hub rollout restart deploy/ea-hub && kubectl -n ea-hub rollout status deploy/ea-hub

# PostgreSQL superuser (bundled database): change it in the database first, then in the Secret
P=$(new)
kubectl -n ea-hub exec ea-hub-postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -qc "alter role postgres with password '$P'"
kubectl -n ea-hub patch secret ea-hub -p "{\"stringData\":{\"postgres-password\":\"$P\"}}"
unset P

CronJobs (backup, cleanup) read the Secret when they run, so they pick up new values without a restart. If you set secrets.* in your values file, change the value there instead and run helm upgrade (the pods restart on their own); for secrets.postgresPassword, run the alter role command above with the new value first. With secrets.existingSecret, update your own Secret (Vault, SealedSecrets…) and restart the deployment.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
A backup runs every day at 01:00 UTC and keeps 14 days (backup.schedule, backup.keepDays). Each backup holds a database dump and the uploaded files. To take one now:

kubectl -n ea-hub create job --from=cronjob/ea-hub-backup backup-now
kubectl -n ea-hub logs job/backup-now -f
# [backup] … saved 2026-12-01_0100 (12M)

Copy backups off the cluster. The chart can copy each backup to object storage right after it is written (rclone: S3, MinIO, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage and others):

backup:
  offsite:
    enabled: true
    path: my-bucket/ea-hub            # bucket/folder (Azure: container/folder)
    config: { type: s3, provider: AWS, region: eu-central-1 }
    credentials: { access_key_id: "…", secret_access_key: "…" }
    # MinIO: config: { type: s3, provider: Minio, endpoint: https://minio.example.com }
    # Azure: config: { type: azureblob, account: mystorage }, credentials: { key: "…" }

Encrypt the backups. Create a key pair once with docker run --rm ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost node selfhost/scripts/backup-crypt.mjs keygen, keep the private key offline, and set backup.encryption.publicKey. Each backup is then encrypted (X25519 and AES-256-GCM, with tampering detected) before it is stored or copied offsite. To restore, first run backup-crypt.mjs decrypt-dir <folder> with BACKUP_PRIVATE_KEY.

Old copies are never deleted from the bucket: set a lifecycle rule there (e.g. delete after 90 days). To restore from the bucket, copy one folder back with rclone copy <remote>:my-bucket/ea-hub/<name> ./<name>, put it on the ea-hub-backups volume, and follow the restore steps.

docs.title: Several app replicas (uploads in S3)
docs.text:
By default, uploads live on a ReadWriteOnce volume, so one app pod runs. To run more replicas, keep uploads in an S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW, Cloudflare R2…):

replicaCount: 2
storage:
  backend: s3
  s3:
    bucket: ea-hub-uploads
    region: eu-central-1
    endpoint: ""                  # e.g. https://minio.example.com for non-AWS services
    accessKeyId: "…"
    secretAccessKey: "…"

Files are still served by the app, so access rules and signed links work exactly as before. The bucket can stay private. With S3, the nightly backup contains the database only: turn on bucket versioning or replication to protect the files. Database migrations are safe with several replicas, because each pod waits for a lock.

docs.title: Monitoring and network policies
docs.text: Value What it does metrics.enabled: true Serves Prometheus metrics at /metrics. A token is generated in the release Secret (metrics-token), and scrapers must send it as Authorization: Bearer … metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled: true Creates a ServiceMonitor for the Prometheus Operator, with the token wired in networkPolicy.enabled: true Only pods of this release may reach PostgreSQL. The app is reachable from the namespaces in networkPolicy.ingressNamespaceSelectors (any namespace when empty) podDisruptionBudget.enabled (on) With replicaCount > 1, keeps one app pod running during node drains metrics.prometheusRule.enabled: true Alerts: app down, database down or slow, high memory, a backup failed, no backup for 2 days (the backup alerts need kube-state-metrics) metrics.grafanaDashboard.enabled: true A Grafana dashboard as a ConfigMap with grafana_dashboard: "1", which the kube-prometheus-stack sidecar loads

docs.title: Autoscaling and tracing
docs.text:
Value What it does autoscaling.enabled: true A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (2–6 pods at 70% CPU by default). Needs storage.backend: s3 or a ReadWriteMany volume tracing.otlpEndpoint: http://otel-collector:4318 One OpenTelemetry span per request, sent over OTLP/HTTP to your collector (Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Azure Monitor…). Continues the caller's traceparent. Exporter headers go in the Secret key otel-headers

Every pull request also runs an OWASP ZAP baseline scan and a k6 load test (25 concurrent users on a 2-vCPU runner) against the full stack.

docs.title: High availability for PostgreSQL (CloudNativePG)
docs.text:
The built-in database is a single pod. For automatic failover, install the CloudNativePG operator once per cluster, then:

postgres:
  cloudnativepg:
    enabled: true
    instances: 3            # 1 primary + 2 streaming replicas
    # backup: { barmanObjectStore: … }   # optional: continuous WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery

The chart then creates a postgresql.cnpg.io Cluster instead of the StatefulSet, and the app connects to its -rw service. CI tests this on kind with 2 instances, including deleting the primary while the app keeps working.

docs.title: Upgrading PostgreSQL to a new major version
docs.text:
Docker Compose: run selfhost/scripts/pg-major-upgrade.sh 17. It takes a backup, keeps the old data volume, starts the new version on an empty volume, restores, and prints the rollback commands. CI tests 16 → 17.

Helm, built-in database: take a backup (backup-now), set postgres.image to the new version on a new release or a new PVC, then restore with backup.sh restore. Never change the major version of an existing data volume in place.

CloudNativePG: follow the operator's major-upgrade procedure (an import into a new Cluster).

docs.title: Restore
docs.text: See docs/backup.md for the full procedure (Arabic, with commands). In short: scale the app to 0, run backup.sh restore <name> in a pod that mounts ea-hub-backups, then scale back to 1.

docs.title: Change a setting
docs.text: Edit my-values.yaml and run the same helm upgrade again. Secrets you did not set keep their generated values.

docs.title: Reset the admin password
docs.text:
helm upgrade ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml \
  --set admin.password='<new-password>' --set admin.resetPassword=true
# after signing in, run it again with --set admin.resetPassword=false

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
helm uninstall ea-hub -n ea-hub          # Path B: kubectl delete -n ea-hub -f ~/ea-hub.yaml

The data volumes (ea-hub-storage, ea-hub-backups, data-ea-hub-postgres-0) and the generated Secret are kept on purpose, so an accidental uninstall loses nothing. To delete everything permanently, including all data:

kubectl delete namespace ea-hub

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
What you see Likely cause Fix Pod stuck in Pending No default StorageClass, or not enough CPU/memory kubectl -n ea-hub describe pod <name> → read Events; see Step 1 ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff No access to the private image Create ghcr-pull (Step 3) and reference it; check the tag exists Stuck at Init:0/1 for minutes Database not ready yet kubectl -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub -c migrate and kubectl -n ea-hub logs ea-hub-postgres-0 Init:CrashLoopBackOff with password authentication failed The database was created with a different password (e.g. the Secret was recreated) Restore the original Secret values (from your Secret backup) ADMIN_PASSWORD must be at least 10 characters Admin password too short Fix it in values/Secret and upgrade again Site loads but the HTTPS certificate is invalid DNS not pointing to the ingress yet, or ports 80/443 closed kubectl describe certificate -n ea-hub; check DNS with nslookup hub.example.com 404 from the ingress controller Wrong ingress.className, or the host differs from the browser address kubectl get ingressclass; make ingress.host match the domain Links or images point to the wrong address appUrl does not match what users type Set appUrl exactly, including https:// and the port, then upgrade "Forgot password" sends nothing SMTP not configured Set smtp.*, then upgrade. Admins can use Reset the admin password above Sign-in refused although the password is right 10 failed attempts within 15 minutes lock that e-mail for a while Wait 15 minutes

Useful commands:

kubectl -n ea-hub get all
kubectl -n ea-hub describe pod <pod-name>
kubectl -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub --tail=200
kubectl -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub -c migrate
kubectl -n ea-hub get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

docs.title: Reference: all settings
docs.text:
Every setting is documented with comments in deploy/helm/ea-hub/values.yaml and validated by values.schema.json. The most used:

Value Default Meaning appUrl http://ea-hub.local Required. Public address of the site admin.email / admin.password empty First admin account (created once) image.repository / image.tag ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost / latest (the chart's appVersion) App image — pin a release tag in production imagePullSecrets [] e.g. [{name: ghcr-pull}] ingress.enabled / host / className / tls / annotations off External access smtp.host / port / secure / user / password / from empty Outgoing e-mail features.openaiApiKey empty Search by meaning features.turnstileSiteKey / turnstileSecretKey empty Bot protection storage.size / storageClass / accessMode 5Gi / default / ReadWriteOnce Uploaded files postgres.enabled true Built-in database; set false and fill externalDatabase.* to use your own PostgreSQL 16+ backup.enabled / schedule / keepDays on / 0 1 * * * / 14 Daily backups cron.schedules.* / cron.timeZone see values Scheduled jobs secrets.create / secrets.existingSecret true / empty Manage secrets yourself (Vault, SealedSecrets…) replicaCount 1 Keep 1 unless storage.accessMode is ReadWriteMany resources see values App CPU/memory

For how the self-hosted version replaces Supabase and Vercel, see docs/architecture.md.

docs.title: Deploying EA-Hub on Red Hat OpenShift (or OKD)
docs.text: OpenShift runs every pod under a random user ID and publishes sites with Routes. The Helm chart has an OpenShift mode that handles both: set openshift.enabled=true.

docs.title: Cluster capacity
docs.text:
Minimum Recommended CPU (requests across the project) 2 vCPU 4 vCPU Memory 4 GiB 8 GiB Persistent storage 35 GiB (ReadWriteOnce): 5 uploads + 10 database + 20 backups 60 GiB

If your project has a ResourceQuota, it must allow at least 4 pods, 3 PVCs and the memory above.

docs.title: Software and access
docs.text: Need Version / detail Check OpenShift Container Platform or OKD 4.14+ (Kubernetes 1.27+) oc version oc CLI matching your cluster oc version --client Helm 3.8+ or 4.x (or use the Developer console, see below) helm version Permission create a project, or admin on an existing one oc auth can-i create deployments -n <project> Default StorageClass any ReadWriteOnce (e.g. gp3-csi, thin-csi, ODF ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd) oc get storageclass Security context the default restricted-v2 SCC is enough; no anyuid or privileged access needed Image access the cluster must be able to pull ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost and docker.io/library/postgres:16. In disconnected clusters, mirror both to your internal registry Domain the cluster's apps domain (e.g. *.apps.cluster.example.com) or your own host name oc get ingresses.config cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.domain}'

docs.title: 2. Log in and create a project
docs.text:
oc login --token=<token> --server=https://api.cluster.example.com:6443   # "Copy login command" in the web console
oc new-project ea-hub

docs.title: 3. Get the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/E20E-Tools/ea-hub-selfhost.git
cd ea-hub-selfhost

docs.title: 4. Make the image available
docs.text:
Use one of these options.

a) Published image (default): ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost is public, so there is nothing to do. You need a pull secret only if your cluster reaches GHCR through an authenticated proxy:

oc create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<github-user> --docker-password=<token-with-read:packages>
oc secrets link default ghcr-pull --for=pull

b) Mirror to your own registry (disconnected clusters):

skopeo copy docker://ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost:<version> docker://registry.internal/ea-hub/ea-hub-selfhost:<version>
skopeo copy docker://docker.io/library/postgres:16 docker://registry.internal/ea-hub/postgres:16

Then use image.repository=registry.internal/ea-hub/ea-hub-selfhost and postgres.image=registry.internal/ea-hub/postgres:16 below.

c) Build inside OpenShift from this repository:

oc new-build --name ea-hub --strategy docker --binary
oc start-build ea-hub --from-dir=. --follow
# image: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/ea-hub/ea-hub:latest

docs.title: 5. Choose the address
docs.text:
Use the default Route host, or your own name:

APPS=$(oc get ingresses.config cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.domain}')
echo "https://ea-hub.$APPS"        # e.g. https://ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com

docs.title: 6. Write your values file
docs.text:
my-values.yaml. Keep it outside the repository, because it holds a password:

appUrl: https://ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com

openshift:
  enabled: true              # random UIDs, Debian postgres image, Route
  route:
    enabled: true
    host: ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com
    tls: true                # edge TLS with the router certificate, HTTP → HTTPS

ingress:
  enabled: false             # the Route replaces the Ingress

admin:
  email: admin@yourcompany.com
  password: choose-a-long-password

image:
  repository: ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost
  tag: "<version>"

# storage:
#   storageClass: thin-csi   # only if there is no default StorageClass
# smtp: { host: smtp.example.com, port: 587, user: …, password: …, from: "EA-Hub <…>" }

What openshift.enabled=true changes in the rendered resources:

  • No runAsUser, runAsGroup or fsGroup is set, so the restricted-v2 SCC assigns them. The EA-Hub image is built to run under any user ID in group 0.
  • PostgreSQL uses postgres:16 (Debian), which supports random user IDs. The Alpine variant is only for plain Kubernetes.
  • A Route with edge TLS is created for the Service.

docs.title: 7. Install
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml
oc -n ea-hub rollout status deploy/ea-hub --timeout=10m
oc -n ea-hub get pods,route

NAME                          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/ea-hub-5b7d9c6f4-8kx2p    1/1     Running   0          3m
pod/ea-hub-postgres-0         1/1     Running   0          3m

NAME                              HOST/PORT                              SERVICES   PORT   TERMINATION
route.route.openshift.io/ea-hub   ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com        ea-hub     http   edge/Redirect

Follow the database setup while the pod shows Init:0/1:

oc -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub -c migrate -f

docs.title: Alternative: the web console (no Helm CLI)
docs.text:
1. Add the EA-Hub chart repository once. For the whole cluster (cluster-admin):
cat <<'EOF' | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: helm.openshift.io/v1beta1
kind: HelmChartRepository
metadata:
  name: ea-hub
spec:
  name: EA-Hub
  connectionConfig:
    url: https://e20e-tools.github.io/ea-hub-selfhost
EOF

For one project only, without cluster-admin, use kind: ProjectHelmChartRepository with metadata.namespace: ea-hub. 2. Install it. Open the Developer perspective, choose project ea-hub, then +Add → Helm Chart and select EA-Hub → Create. The form is built from the chart's schema. Set appUrl, admin.email and openshift.enabled: true. The chart page also has a Test action that runs helm test and calls /healthz. 3. Or +Add → Import YAML and paste the output of helm template ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml. This has no upgrade tracking; the Helm CLI is preferred.

docs.title: 8. Open the site and sign in
docs.text:
Open https://ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com/admin:

Health check: curl https://ea-hub.apps.cluster.example.com/healthz returns {"ok":true,"database":"ok"}.

docs.title: 9. Operations
docs.text:
Task Command Upgrade helm upgrade ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml --set image.tag=<new> Backup now oc -n ea-hub create job --from=cronjob/ea-hub-backup backup-now Logs oc -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub -f Back up the generated secrets oc -n ea-hub get secret ea-hub -o yaml > ea-hub-secret-backup.yaml (store it safely) Uninstall (keeps data) helm uninstall ea-hub -n ea-hub Delete everything oc delete project ea-hub

Your own certificate on the Route: install the cert-manager Operator plus the openshift-routes add-on, and set openshift.route.annotations: {cert-manager.io/issuer-name: …}. Or ask your cluster administrator for the router's wildcard certificate, which is used automatically.

docs.title: Alternative: the EA-Hub operator
docs.text:
Instead of Helm you can install the EA-Hub operator (Operator Lifecycle Manager). It runs the same chart: each EAHub resource is one installation and its spec holds the chart values from step 6.

Until the operator is listed in OperatorHub, install it from the bundle image of a release (needs operator-sdk):

operator-sdk run bundle ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-operator-bundle:<version> -n ea-hub-operator

Then create the installation (no passwords in the spec: they are generated into the Secret ea-hub):

cat <<'EOF' | oc apply -n ea-hub -f -
apiVersion: ea-hub.e20e-tools.github.io/v1alpha1
kind: EAHub
metadata:
  name: ea-hub
spec:
  appUrl: https://ea-hub.apps.example.com
  admin: { email: admin@example.com }
  openshift: { enabled: true }
EOF
oc -n ea-hub get eahub                      # DEPLOYED True
oc -n ea-hub get secret ea-hub -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d

Change a setting with oc -n ea-hub edit eahub ea-hub; the operator upgrades the release. Deleting the EAHub removes the installation; the Secret with the generated passwords is kept.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix unable to validate against any security context constraint openshift.enabled is not true. The default mode sets fixed UIDs that restricted-v2 refuses PostgreSQL CrashLoopBackOff: could not change permissions of directory You overrode postgres.image with an image that cannot run under a random UID. Use postgres:16 (Debian) or a mirror of it ImagePullBackOff Link the pull secret (oc secrets link default ghcr-pull --for=pull) or mirror the images (step 4) PVC Pending There is no default StorageClass: set storage.storageClass, postgres.storage.storageClass and backup.storage.storageClass Route shows "Application is not available" The pod is not ready yet: oc -n ea-hub get pods, then read the migrate logs Quota exceeded Ask for a larger quota, or lower resources / postgres.resources in your values

docs.title: Deploying EA-Hub with Rancher
docs.text: Rancher manages Kubernetes clusters (RKE2, K3s, or imported AKS/EKS/GKE). EA-Hub installs on a Rancher-managed cluster with the same Helm chart, and you can do everything from the Rancher web UI.

docs.title: Downstream cluster (where EA-Hub runs)
docs.text: Minimum Recommended Kubernetes 1.27+ (RKE2 or K3s) latest supported by your Rancher version Worker capacity 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM free 4 vCPU, 8 GB Storage a default StorageClass with 35 GB free (local-path on K3s, Longhorn, vSphere CSI, cloud disks…) Longhorn or your cloud's CSI with snapshots Ingress controller RKE2 ships ingress-nginx (class nginx); K3s ships Traefik (class traefik) HTTPS (optional) cert-manager (Rancher → Apps → Charts → cert-manager) or your own certificate

docs.title: Rancher and your workstation
docs.text: Need Detail Rancher Manager 2.8 or newer, with a user that is Project Owner/Member on the target cluster One of these the Rancher kubectl shell in the browser (has kubectl and helm built in), or kubectl + Helm on your PC with the cluster's kubeconfig Image access the cluster can pull ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost (with a pull secret if the package is private) or a copy in your registry DNS a host name (e.g. hub.example.com) pointing to the cluster's ingress / load balancer

docs.title: 2. Open a shell on the cluster
docs.text:
From the browser: Rancher → ☰ → Cluster Management → your cluster → Explore → the >_ Kubectl Shell button at the top right. helm and kubectl are already available there.

From your PC: Explore → the ⋮ menu → Download KubeConfig, then:

export KUBECONFIG=~/Downloads/<cluster>.yaml
kubectl get nodes

docs.title: 3. Create a Project and Namespace (Rancher UI)
docs.text: Explore → Cluster → Projects/Namespaces → Create Project ea-hub → Create Namespace ea-hub inside it. With the CLI, kubectl create namespace ea-hub also works; then move the namespace into a project in the UI.

docs.title: 4. Image pull secret (only if the image is private)
docs.text:
Rancher UI: Explore → Storage → Secrets → Create → Registry. Namespace ea-hub, name ghcr-pull, registry ghcr.io, username = your GitHub user, password = a token with read:packages.

CLI equivalent:

kubectl -n ea-hub create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<github-user> --docker-password=<token>

docs.title: 5. Get the chart
docs.text:
In the kubectl shell or on your PC:

git clone https://github.com/E20E-Tools/ea-hub-selfhost.git
cd ea-hub-selfhost

docs.title: 6. Write your values
docs.text:
my-values.yaml:

appUrl: https://hub.example.com
admin:
  email: admin@yourcompany.com
  password: choose-a-long-password
image:
  repository: ghcr.io/e20e-tools/ea-hub-selfhost
  tag: "<version>"
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: ghcr-pull                 # remove if not needed
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx                  # RKE2. Use traefik on K3s
  host: hub.example.com
  tls: true
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt   # if cert-manager is installed
# Longhorn example:
# storage: { storageClass: longhorn }
# postgres: { storage: { storageClass: longhorn } }
# backup: { storage: { storageClass: longhorn } }

docs.title: 7. Install
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml
kubectl -n ea-hub rollout status deploy/ea-hub --timeout=10m

In the Rancher UI, under Explore → Apps → Installed Apps, the release ea-hub appears with its status. Workloads shows the ea-hub Deployment, the ea-hub-postgres StatefulSet and the CronJobs.

docs.title: Alternatives inside Rancher
docs.text: Method When How Apps → Charts (recommended, no CLI) Any Rancher 2.6+ version Apps → Repositories → Create → Target: http(s) URL to an index generated by Helm → Index URL https://e20e-tools.github.io/ea-hub-selfhost → Create. Then Apps → Charts → EA-Hub → Install. Rancher shows a form with sections for General, Access, Storage, E-mail and Optional features (site address, admin e-mail, Ingress, volume sizes, SMTP, optional keys). Leave the admin password empty to generate one: the release notes in Installed Apps show the command that reads it Apps → Charts from an OCI repository Rancher 2.9+ Same as above with Target: OCI and oci://ghcr.io/e20e-tools/charts Import YAML No Helm at all Run helm template ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml > ea-hub.yaml on any machine, then cluster ⬆ Import YAML → paste → namespace ea-hub. Or use deploy/kubernetes/ea-hub.yaml with your Secret, as in deploy-kubernetes.md Continuous Delivery (Fleet, GitOps) Several clusters, changes through Git Add a GitRepo pointing at this repository with path deploy/helm/ea-hub. Keep your values in a Kubernetes Secret and reference it with helm.valuesFrom in a fleet.yaml in your own config repository

docs.title: 8. DNS and HTTPS
docs.text:
1. Find the ingress address: Explore → Service Discovery → Ingresses → ea-hub, or kubectl -n ea-hub get ingress.
  2. Create a DNS A record hub.example.com → that address (or your load balancer's).
  3. With cert-manager and the letsencrypt ClusterIssuer (see deploy-kubernetes.md, step 4), the certificate is issued automatically. Without cert-manager, create a TLS secret named ea-hub-tls in Explore → Storage → Secrets → TLS Certificate.

docs.title: 9. Open the site and sign in
docs.text: Open https://hub.example.com/admin:

docs.title: 10. Operations from Rancher
docs.text: Task Rancher UI CLI Logs Workloads → ea-hub → ⋮ → View Logs (choose container migrate or app) kubectl -n ea-hub logs deploy/ea-hub -f Backup now Workloads → CronJobs → ea-hub-backup → ⋮ → Run Now kubectl -n ea-hub create job --from=cronjob/ea-hub-backup backup-now Upgrade Apps → Installed Apps → ea-hub → Upgrade (OCI method) helm upgrade ea-hub deploy/helm/ea-hub -n ea-hub -f my-values.yaml --set image.tag=<new> Monitoring Install the Monitoring app; pod CPU/memory appear under Workloads Volume snapshots Longhorn UI → Volumes → ea-hub-* → snapshot/backup schedule Uninstall (keeps data) Apps → Installed Apps → ⋮ → Delete helm uninstall ea-hub -n ea-hub

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Fix Ingress returns 404 Wrong ingress.className: nginx on RKE2, traefik on K3s (kubectl get ingressclass) PVC Pending No default StorageClass: set it in Rancher (Storage → StorageClasses → ⋮ → Set as Default) or pass storageClass values Pods blocked by Pod Security Admission The chart runs non-root with seccomp RuntimeDefault and drops all capabilities, so it fits the restricted policy; check any custom PSA/Kyverno/Gatekeeper rule ImagePullBackOff The pull secret must be in namespace ea-hub and named in imagePullSecrets

The rest is identical to the generic guide: deploy-kubernetes.md.

docs.title: Single sign-on (OpenID Connect)
docs.text:
EA-Hub can let people sign in with their organisation account through any OpenID Connect provider: Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, Google Workspace, Authentik, Ping and others. Password sign-in keeps working next to it.

When single sign-on is configured, the admin sign-in page shows a Sign in with your organisation account button.

docs.title: How access is decided
docs.text:
Person What happens at sign-in E-mail domain not in OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS (when that list is set) Refused Verified e-mail listed in OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS, or member of a group in OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS Signed in. The account is created if needed and gets the admin role Already has an EA-Hub account with the same verified e-mail Signed in to that account. Roles are unchanged Anyone else Refused, unless OIDC_AUTO_CREATE=true and OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS is set. Then an account without roles is created

Other rules:

  • Verified e-mail only: EA-Hub uses an e-mail address to find or create an account only when the provider confirms that address. It accepts either of two claims:
  • email_verified set to true.
  • Microsoft Entra ID's xms_edov set to true, meaning the e-mail's domain is verified in your tenant.
  • Unverified e-mails: if your provider confirms neither, you can set OIDC_REQUIRE_VERIFIED_EMAIL=false, but only together with OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS. Unverified addresses are then never linked to an existing account and never match OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS: only OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS can make someone an admin.
  • Limit the domains: always set OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS to your own domains. This matters most with shared issuers such as Google (https://accounts.google.com), which signs in any Google account.
  • Admin rights are only added: they are never removed automatically. To take admin rights away, remove the role in EA-Hub.
  • Offboarding: disabling someone at the provider stops new sign-ins at once, but an open EA-Hub session lasts until its refresh token expires (up to 30 days). To end it immediately, block the user in EA-Hub or remove the account.
  • Security checks:
  • The sign-in uses the authorization code flow with PKCE, state and nonce.
  • The ID token signature is checked against the provider's published keys, along with the issuer, audience and expiry.
  • The redirect URI is fixed to your APP_URL.

docs.title: 1. Register EA-Hub at your provider
docs.text:
Each provider needs the same three things:

  • Application type: web application (confidential client), authorization code flow.
  • Redirect URI: https://<your EA-Hub address>/api/selfhost/auth/oidc/callback, for example https://hub.example.com/api/selfhost/auth/oidc/callback.
  • Scopes: openid email profile, plus a groups claim if you use OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS.

Note the issuer URL, the client ID and the client secret.

Provider Issuer URL Notes Microsoft Entra ID https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0 App registrations → New registration, platform Web, then add a client secret. In Token configuration → Add optional claim → ID, add email and xms_edov. For groups, use Add groups claim: Entra sends group object IDs, so put those IDs in OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS Keycloak https://<keycloak>/realms/<realm> Create a client with Client authentication on and Standard flow on. For groups, add a Group Membership mapper with token claim name groups and Full group path off Okta https://<your-org>.okta.com (or a custom authorization server URL) Create an OIDC – Web Application. For groups, add a groups claim to the ID token Google Workspace https://accounts.google.com Create an OAuth client ID of type Web application. Google sends no groups claim, so use OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS Authentik https://<authentik>/application/o/<app-slug> Create an OAuth2/OpenID Provider with client type Confidential

docs.title: 2. Configure EA-Hub
docs.text:
Docker Compose: add to .env, then run docker compose up -d:

OIDC_ISSUER=https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/v2.0
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret>
OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS=yourcompany.com
OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS=you@yourcompany.com
OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS=                     # optional

Helm:

sso:
  oidc:
    issuer: https://kc.example.com/realms/acme
    clientId: ea-hub
    clientSecret: "<client secret>"     # or key oidc-client-secret in secrets.existingSecret
    allowedDomains: acme.com
    adminGroups: ea-admins
    # adminEmails: you@acme.com

Container-as-a-Service platforms: set the same OIDC_* environment variables. Keep OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET in the platform's secret store.

docs.title: 3. Try it
docs.text: Open https://<your address>/admin, then click Sign in with your organisation account. After your provider's sign-in page, you land back in the admin console.

docs.title: All settings
docs.text: Variable Helm value Default Meaning OIDC_ISSUER sso.oidc.issuer – Provider issuer URL. EA-Hub reads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration OIDC_CLIENT_ID sso.oidc.clientId – Client ID OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET sso.oidc.clientSecret – Client secret. It is sent with HTTP Basic authentication to the token endpoint OIDC_SCOPES sso.oidc.scopes openid email profile Requested scopes OIDC_BUTTON_LABEL sso.oidc.buttonLabel Sign in with your organisation account Button text OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS sso.oidc.adminEmails – Comma-separated e-mails that get the admin role OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS sso.oidc.adminGroups – Comma-separated groups whose members get the admin role OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM sso.oidc.groupsClaim groups ID token claim that lists groups OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS sso.oidc.allowedDomains – Comma-separated e-mail domains allowed to sign in (recommended) OIDC_AUTO_CREATE sso.oidc.autoCreate false Create accounts, without roles, for anyone from OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS OIDC_REQUIRE_VERIFIED_EMAIL sso.oidc.requireVerifiedEmail true Require email_verified (or Entra xms_edov) to be true

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Message on the sign-in page Cause Your organisation account has no access to EA-Hub yet The person has no EA-Hub account and is not listed as an admin, or their e-mail domain is not in OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS. Create the account in EA-Hub, or list them Your organisation did not confirm your e-mail address The ID token has neither email_verified=true nor xms_edov=true. On Entra ID, add the xms_edov optional claim Single sign-on did not complete Check the app logs for [selfhost] SSO sign-in failed:. Common causes are a redirect URI that differs from APP_URL, a wrong client secret, or a clock more than 2 minutes off Single sign-on is unavailable EA-Hub could not reach <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration. Check the issuer URL and outbound network access
